At Eid the Prophet told women to give alms, as he saw most of Hell's dwellers were women, and tied their deficiency in intelligence and religion to testimony and menses.
Men should not stop women going to the mosque, even at night; women left first after the Taslim, unrecognised in Fajr's dark; Umm Sulaim stood behind Anas and an orphan.
Women should be allowed to mosques at night; a wife of Umar kept praying Fajr and Isha there, as the Prophet forbade stopping Allah's women-slaves from Allah's mosques.
A woman should not travel for more than three days, or in another narration a day and night, except with a mahram or her husband.
Umar let the Prophet's wives make Hajj; Hajj is women's best jihad; women travel only with a mahram; a woman who missed Hajj was told to make Umrah in Ramadan.
Women's jihad is Hajj; Umm Haram asks to join the sea fighters; the Prophet draws lots among his wives; women carry water, treat the wounded, bring back the dead.
No man may be alone with a woman, nor a woman travel without a mahram; a man enlisted for a campaign is told to go on Hajj with his wife.
But for Israelites meat would not decay, and but for Eve wives would not betray husbands; treat women kindly, for woman is created from a rib that breaks if straightened.
The Prophet says that if evil omen exists it is in the woman, the house and the horse, and that he leaves men no trial more severe than women.
Woman is like a rib that breaks if straightened, so the Prophet urges care for women; Ibn Umar says men spoke freely with their wives only after the Prophet's death.
The best women among camel riders are of Quraysh, the righteous of them kind to their young children and careful of their husbands' property.
The Prophet told Anjasha to drive slowly the camels of his wives and Um Sulaim, as they carried glass vessels, a phrase Abu Qalaba said others would be blamed for.
On a journey the Prophet told his black slave Anjasha, driving fast the camels women rode, to drive slowly with the glass vessels.
With Um Sulaim among the women in charge of the luggage, the Prophet told Anjash, his slave driving their camels fast, to drive slowly with the glass vessels.
On a journey the Prophet told Anjasha, whose chanting drove the camels fast, to drive slowly and not break the glass vessels, meaning the women.
The verse forbidding inheriting women against their will concerns a pre-Islamic custom whereby a dead man's relatives could marry his wife, marry her off or stop her marrying.
